broccoli-cauliflower-and-carrots-cooked-.title: Broccoli, cauliflower and carrots, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli, cauliflower and carrots are three vegetables often combined in cooking. When cooked by steaming or boiling with a small amount of added fat (oil or butter) they retain most of their vitamins and minerals, and the fat enhances absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli and cauliflower belong to the cruciferous family and are rich in glucosinolates that support liver detoxification.
Carrots are one of the richest sources of beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
This vegetable trio is common in traditional dishes worldwide, from French ratatouille to Asian stir‑fries.
Adding fat can increase the bioavailability of carotenoids in carrots up to 10‑12 times.
Short cooking times (5‑7 minutes) preserve more than 90 % of vitamin C in broccoli.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phytochemicals such as sulforaphane in broccoli and quercetin in cauliflower help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports vision
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots converts to vitamin A, essential for eye health.

items.title: May reduce cardiovascular risk
items.content: Fiber and potassium aid normal blood pressure, while monounsaturated fats from oil support healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C in broccoli and cauliflower enhances immune cell function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber from all three vegetables promotes gut motility and feeds beneficial gut microbes.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to broccoli or cauliflower.

items.title: Excess added fat
items.content: Using too much oil increases the dish’s calorie density and may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Vitamin C loss with prolonged boiling
items.content: Cooking vegetables for more than 10 minutes can degrade a portion of vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the vegetables as a side dish, add them to salads, stews or pasta. Steam for 5‑7 minutes, then lightly sauté with 1‑2 teaspoons of oil. Finish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Store the cooked mixture in an airtight container for up to 3 days.

fruit-and-vegetable-smoothie-no-dairy.title: Fruit and Vegetable Smoothie, No Dairy

content.title: About
content.content: A fruit and vegetable smoothie without dairy is a beverage made from fresh fruits, vegetables, and plant‑based liquids (water, coconut water, plant milks). It contains no dairy ingredients, making it suitable for lactose‑intolerant individuals and vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Smoothies retain most of the vitamins and minerals from the raw produce because they are not heat‑treated.
Adding leafy greens such as spinach or kale barely changes the taste but dramatically boosts nutritional value.
Acai and pomegranate blends are often marketed as “superfood” smoothies due to their high antioxidant content.
For a creamier texture, avocado or frozen bananas are used instead of dairy.
Smoothies can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, though flavor and nutrient levels are best right after blending.

items.title: Rich in vitamins C and A
items.content: Fruits and vegetables like carrots, bell peppers, and citrus provide vitamin C and provitamin A, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber from the produce aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of dairy keeps saturated fat low, which is beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A large water component and electrolytes from coconut water help maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Berries (blueberry, raspberry) and leafy greens contain polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Using too many sweet fruits can raise the smoothie’s glycemic index, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some add‑ins (nuts, chia seeds) can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: A large amount of fiber in one serving may cause bloating or loose stools in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Metallic taste
items.content: Blending acidic ingredients (lemon, lime) in metal containers can cause slight oxidation, affecting flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the smoothie immediately after blending. It can also be poured into a bowl and topped with granola, nuts, seeds, or fresh berries. For a more filling version, add protein powder or rolled oats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared smoothie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. For longer storage, portion it out and freeze; thaw in the fridge before drinking and give it a quick shake.

rice-white-with-dark-green-vegetables-an.title: White Rice with Dark Green Vegetables and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice combined with dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach) and tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce. The combination provides a balanced mix of carbohydrates, fiber, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple source of energy in many cultures worldwide.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells.
The dish can be easily adapted to different cuisines by changing spices and the type of sauce.
When cooked properly, rice retains most of its nutritional value.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: White rice provides a quick source of glucose needed for brain and muscle function.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are involved in carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients from vegetables
items.content: Dark green vegetables add dietary fiber, vitamin K, iron, and calcium.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and chlorophyll from vegetables help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C in tomatoes boosts the body’s immune response.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain green vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a side or a main course. Add herbs, spices, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of water to prevent drying out.
